common_name: Munchkin Oakleaf Hydrangea (True Dwarf Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Munchkin is a true dwarf oakleaf hydrangea, staying noticeably smaller than compact cultivars like Pee Wee or Sikes Dwarf and well suited to small beds and containers.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, with protection from hot afternoon sun in the Deep South. Munchkin is one of the smallest oakleaf hydrangea cultivars available, bred to bring the bold, deeply lobed foliage and cone-shaped white flower panicles of the species down to a true dwarf scale suited to small gardens, foundation plantings, and large containers where a full-sized oakleaf hydrangea would quickly outgrow the space. Flower panicles open white in early summer and age to a soft pink, and the compact plant still develops the rich burgundy and orange fall foliage color and exfoliating bark the species is known for. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering, since next year's flower buds form on the current season's growth by late summer, and avoid pruning in fall, winter, or spring, which removes the coming year's blooms.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Oakleaf Hydrangea Cultivars
North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

common_name: Amethyst Oakleaf Hydrangea (Dark Purple-Red Reblooming Oakleaf)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Amethyst is grown for flower panicles that age to an unusually deep purple-red compared with the pink or rose tones of most other oakleaf hydrangea cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun. Amethyst is an oakleaf hydrangea selected for flower panicles that mature to a deep, saturated purple-red unusually dark for the species, extending the multi-season color display well beyond the typical white-to-pink progression of most oakleaf cultivars. The bold, deeply lobed foliage turns rich burgundy and orange in fall, and the exfoliating cinnamon bark adds winter interest once leaves drop. Prune, if needed, right after flowering, since flower buds for the following year set on the current season's growth by late summer, and avoid cutting back in fall, winter, or spring, which removes next year's bloom.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Oakleaf Hydrangea Cultivars
North Carolina State Extension — Hydrangea Species and Cultivars

common_name: Gatsby Moon Oakleaf Hydrangea (Large Double-Flowered Oakleaf Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gatsby Moon is part of the Gatsby series bred for extra-large, heavily double flower panicles on a full-sized oakleaf hydrangea shrub.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade, giving this full-sized cultivar plenty of room to reach its mature spread. Gatsby Moon is part of the Gatsby series of oakleaf hydrangeas bred for exceptionally large, densely double, pure white flower panicles that age to a soft pink, giving an especially showy, full-looking bloom compared with the single-flowered species. The bold, deeply lobed foliage turns outstanding shades of burgundy, orange, and purple in fall, and the exfoliating cinnamon bark provides winter interest after leaf drop. Prune, if needed, immediately after flowering, since next year's flower buds form on the current season's growth by late summer, and avoid pruning in fall, winter, or spring, which removes the coming year's blooms.

common_name: Raydon's Favorite Aster (Drought-Tolerant Native Aromatic Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Raydon's Favorite is one of the most widely planted aromatic aster cultivars, prized for exceptional drought tolerance and a dense, floriferous fall display.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Raydon's Favorite is a beloved selection of native aromatic aster, forming a dense, rounded mound of fragrant gray-green foliage that becomes smothered in masses of small, violet-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers in fall, providing an important late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and other pollinators when few other perennials are still blooming. It is exceptionally tolerant of heat, drought, and poor soil once established, thriving with minimal supplemental water even through Gulf South summers, and resists the powdery mildew that troubles many other asters in humid climates. Cut the plant back by about half in late spring to keep growth compact and promote the fullest fall bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
